newsitem.title: USA: Blair may attend Hong Kong handover, Cook says.
newsitem.headline: Blair may attend Hong Kong handover, Cook says.

text.p: New British Prime Minister Tony Blair is considering attending ceremonies marking the handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1, British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Monday.
Cook, on a one-day visit to Washington, told a news conference he himself would attend and added: "We are exploring the ability of Mr Blair to be present at the handover ceremony."

Cook was speaking after talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who announced earlier she would attend the ceremony in a clear sign of U.S. support for the maintenance of civil liberties in the territory under Chinese rule.

Cook said the Labour government, which took power after defeating the Conservatives in the May 1 election, would honour the previous Conservative government's commitment to make six-monthly reports on the state of human rights in Hong Kong.
Cook said he was confident after discussing this issue with Albright and other State Department and Congressional figures that Britain would get U.S. cooperation in following up on those reports.

He said he stressed with all the U.S. officials he met Britain's "very strong interest" in Hong Kong after the handover to ensure that China fulfils commitments it has made to maintain civil rights and financial freedoms.
"We will be looking for United States support to make sure that those agreements with China are honoured," he said.

But he said whatever pressure Washington might bring to bear should not include suspension of Beijing's Most Favoured Nation trading status, which he said was vital for the continued prosperity of Hong Kong.
"It would not help to protect Hong Kong if any measure was taken by the United States which undermined the economy of Hong Kong," Cook said.
President Bill Clinton announced on Monday he was renewing MFN, but intensive debate was expected in the coming weeks in Congress, which has the right to reverse that decision.

Clinton's National Security adviser, Samuel (Sandy) Berger told reporters after Clinton's announcement: "Underdcutting the island's footing at this moment would be a serious blow just at a time when Hong Kong needs to assert its strength and its autonomy."
He added: "We must support the economic vitality of Hong Kong during this period of transition."
